definition.text: The part of a soil made of particles 2 mm across or smaller.

facts.text: In the WRB the whole soil comprises the fine earth plus coarse fragments, artefacts, cemented parts and dead plant residues of any size.
Many WRB horizon criteria are stated as percentages by volume related to the fine earth, such as the share of rock structure in an A or B horizon.
Where feldspars weather slowly in cool climates on granite, sand comes to dominate the fine-earth fraction.
A loam can lose its desirable qualities when clay is dispersed throughout its fine-earth fraction.

title: Loss on ignition

definition.text: A test that strongly heats a soil or mineral sample at a set temperature until its mass stops changing, so the weight lost measures the volatile components driven off.

facts.text: A few grams go into a tared, pre-ignited crucible, are weighed, heated in a temperature-controlled furnace for a set time, cooled in a dry, CO2-free atmosphere and weighed again.
The furnace temperature is chosen for the component sought; the mass lost equals the mass of that component.
A sample left overnight in a drying oven at 100 °C loses all its water, giving the dry weight and so the original water content.
It is typically used to estimate water content, carbon, organic matter and volatile compounds; in minerals the loss is mostly combined water and carbon dioxide from carbonates.
Weighing samples taken down a profile before and after burning off their organic content gives organic content at each depth.
A sudden rise in organic content down a profile, with other indicators, is strong evidence for a buried soil surface not visible to the eye.
Monitoring mass continuously as the temperature changes is a variant called thermogravimetry.

notes: Geoarchaeology#Loss on Ignition Testing sentences (bd32c8d1f8c6 section) supply the buried-horizon facts.

definition.text: A wet-chemistry method that measures the organic nitrogen plus ammonia and ammonium in a sample.

facts.text: The sample is digested in concentrated sulfuric acid at 360–410 °C, which oxidizes the organic matter and holds the reduced nitrogen as ammonium sulfate.
Sodium hydroxide then turns the ammonium into ammonia gas, which is distilled into a standard acid and measured by titration.
Without modification it misses other inorganic nitrogen such as nitrate.
Total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN) is the sum of organic, ammonia and ammonium nitrogen in analyses of soil, water and waste water.
Besides foods, it is used to assay soils, waste waters and fertilizers.
Catalysts such as selenium, Hg2SO4 or CuSO4 speed digestion, and Na2SO4 or K2SO4 raises the acid's boiling point.
Its hot concentrated acid and testing time of an hour or more compare poorly with the faster Dumas method.

title: Elemental analysis

definition.text: Analysis of a material such as soil for its elemental, and sometimes isotopic, composition.

facts.text: The commonest form, CHNS analysis, is done by combustion analysis, burning the sample and measuring the oxidized products.
CHN analyzers use the Dumas method's flash combustion and detect the resulting gases by thermal conductivity or infrared.
In the Dumas method a sample is burned at 800–900 °C in oxygen, and gas chromatography separates the released nitrogen for a thermal conductivity detector.
Dumas analysis takes a few minutes per measurement, against an hour or more for Kjeldahl, and uses no toxic chemicals or catalysts.

notes: Folds the Dumas method and Combustion analysis pages, which have no soil sentences of their own.

definition.text: The use of ammonium acetate solution in soil analysis to displace exchangeable cations, for measuring CEC and available potassium.

facts.text: The ammonium ion acts as a replacement cation, displacing potassium from exchange sites.
Ammonium is one of the cations frequently used to displace a soil's bound cations when measuring CEC.
A pure ammonium acetate solution has a pH of about 7, but it buffers only around pH 4.75 and 9.25, not at pH 7.

verification.title: Addressing a Common Misconception: Ammonium Acetate as Neutral pH “Buffer” for Native Electrospray Mass Spectrometry
verification.venue: Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry
verification.evidence: Ammonium acetate does provide buffering around pH 4.75 (the pK a of acetic acid) and around pH 9.25 (the pK a of ammonium).
A 0.2% solution of alpha,alpha-dipyridyl dissolved in 1N ammonium acetate (NH 4OAc) pH 7 can verify the presence of Fe+2 in the field (Childs, 1981).
Ratio, CEC-7 to clay.—A calculation that is used to define the relationship between measured cation- exchange capacity (by ammonium acetate at pH7) and silicate clay.

definition.text: An elemental analysis method that measures the concentration of metals in a sample from the light their atoms absorb.

facts.text: Metals are vaporized in a flame; each absorbs at its own wavelengths, and the absorbed radiation is proportional to the density of its atoms.
Soil extracts from batch equilibration are commonly analysed by atomic absorption, among other methods.
Flame AAS works in the mg/L range; graphite-furnace AAS is 2–3 orders of magnitude more sensitive.
Its modern form was developed in the 1950s by Alan Walsh's team at CSIRO in Melbourne; it is used from agriculture to medicine.

title: Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy
article: Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy

definition.text: An analytical technique (ICP-AES or ICP-OES) that detects chemical elements from the light emitted by atoms and ions excited in an argon plasma.

facts.text: The plasma runs at 6000 to 10,000 K, and the intensity emitted at each element's wavelengths is proportional to its concentration.
A pump feeds the sample to a nebulizer, which sprays it as a mist directly into the plasma.
Detector arrays read all wavelengths at once, so every element the unit can sense is analysed simultaneously and quickly.
Concentrations come from comparing line intensities with calibration curves of known standards.
It is fast becoming the method of choice for nutrient levels in agricultural soils, used to calculate the fertiliser needed for yield and quality.
It is often used for trace elements in soil, and so in forensics to trace the origin of soil found at crime scenes.
It has largely replaced older methods such as gravimetric analysis for routine multi-element trace analysis.

definition.text: Mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) that ionizes a sample in an inductively coupled plasma and counts the resulting ions to detect metals and some non-metals at very low concentrations.

facts.text: It is faster, more precise and more sensitive than atomic absorption, and it scans all elements at once rather than one at a time.
It covers atomic masses 7 to 250 (Li to U) over a dynamic range from 1 part per quadrillion to 100 ppm, and distinguishes isotopes.
Environmental uses run from water testing to analysis of soil and other materials.
Measuring Fe2+ and Fe3+ in ancient rocks with ICP-MS or X-ray fluorescence reveals the redox potential of ancient soils.

definition.text: Chromatography that separates ions and ionizable molecules by their affinity for an ion exchanger.

facts.text: Anion-exchange columns carry a positive stationary phase that holds anions; cation-exchange columns a negative one that holds cations.
It is a popular method for anions and complexes in environmental problems and is one of the methods used to analyse soil extracts.
Its origins trace to Thompson and Way, who treated clays with fertilizer salts and found ammonia retained and calcium released.

definition.text: A membrane-based potentiometric sensor that converts the activity of a specific ion in solution into an electrical potential.

facts.text: Its voltage depends on the logarithm of the ion's activity, following the Nernst equation, and is read against a reference electrode.
The pH glass electrode is a very common type.
Ion-specific electrodes are among the methods used to analyse soil extracts, and their use extends to environmental science and agriculture.
Readings drift with temperature and time, so frequent recalibration against standards is needed, ideally before and after each sample.

title: Molybdenum blue phosphate test
article: Molybdenum blue#Colorimetric determination of P, As, Si and Ge

definition.text: A colorimetric test in which phosphate forms a blue molybdenum complex whose depth of colour is proportional to phosphorus concentration.

facts.text: Phosphate is mixed with an acid molybdate solution and the complex is reduced, for example by ascorbic acid, to the blue form.
However phosphorus is brought from soil into solution, it is usually detected this way, with a colorimeter in the lab or detector sticks and a colour chart in the field.
Comparable amounts of arsenate spoil the test, since arsenate behaves much like phosphate.
Soil phosphate mapped on archaeological plans shows former activity areas and helps prospect for sites.

notes: Detection facts from Geoarchaeology#Phosphate and Orthophosphate Content with Spectrophotometry.

definition.text: Chromatography that separates and analyses compounds that can be vaporized without decomposing.

facts.text: It is used to measure chemicals in soil, air or water, including soil gases.
The Dumas nitrogen method ends with a gas chromatography column that separates nitrogen from carbon dioxide and water.

definition.text: Controls or standards of known composition used to check the quality and traceability of measurements, validate methods and calibrate instruments.

facts.text: Most analytical instruments are comparative, so they need a sample of known composition for accurate calibration.
A certified material differs from a laboratory reagent in its certificate: it gives the value, its uncertainty and a statement of metrological traceability.
Accreditation under ISO/IEC 17025 requires traceability to certified reference materials where possible, and they are preferred where available.
ILAC lists five types: pure substances, standard solutions and gas mixtures, matrix materials, physico-chemical materials, and reference objects.
Natural matrix materials are made by homogenizing a natural sample to a fine powder, since natural materials are rarely homogeneous at the gram scale, then measuring each analyte.
Producers test homogeneity on 10-30 randomly chosen units with two or three subsamples each, and test stability by real-time or accelerated storage studies.

definition.text: The treatment a sample receives before analysis so that it is in a form the instrument can measure.

facts.text: It matters because techniques are often unresponsive to the analyte in its in-situ form, or results are distorted by interfering species.
Steps can include crushing and dissolution, acid or alkali digestion, extraction, clean-up and pre-concentration.
It may also involve pulverizing, filtering, dilution, masking, sub-sampling or treatment with a chelating agent such as EDTA.

definition.text: Collecting a representative composite of soil cores from a field so a laboratory can evaluate fertility.

facts.text: Samples for general fertility are usually taken in fall or spring before the season, analysed for pH, lime requirement, P, K, Ca and Mg; repeat at the same season and with the same lab for comparable years.
Take cores from at least 15-20 random spots per field or zone, whatever its size; one sample should represent no more than 10-20 acres, or 1-5 acres for precision zone or grid management.
Sample between rows, avoid old fence rows and dead furrows, and sample problem areas separately, since nutrient levels vary with crop history and topography.
Sample cultivated fields to plow depth, permanent pasture to 3 or 4 inches, and no-till fields twice: 6 inches for lime and fertilizer advice and 2 inches to monitor surface acidity.
Mix the cores in a clean container, remove roots and stones and air dry; sample fields at least every three years.

sources.title: 21.2: Taking Soil Samples - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: The multi-year matching of a soil test value to crop yield response, which is what makes the test value meaningful.

facts.text: Soil tests estimate a few nutrients from a small sample meant to represent many acres, so they are not 100% accurate.
Researchers apply different nutrient levels (always including zero) to plots on many fields over several years and compare yields to learn what a test level means.
A new test cannot be called useful until it has been correlated with plant response on varied soils and weather, and small-plot results must be validated on commercial farms.

A low test may fail to raise yield if it is poorly calibrated for that soil or if drainage or compaction harms the crop; extra nutrients on a high-testing soil occasionally help when weather reduces availability.

sources.title: 21.3: Accuracy of Recommendations Based on Soil Tests - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: Regional chemical extractions used to estimate plant-available phosphorus, with different numeric ranges for each extractant.

facts.text: The extractant varies by region: Olsen and AB-DTPA in arid and semiarid western areas, Mehlich 3 or Bray 1 in the humid Midwest and East, Mehlich 1 in the Southeast and mid-Atlantic, Morgan in the Northeast.
Bray 1 is used for acidic soils and Olsen for alkaline soils in Washington and Oregon.
Ranges for the optimum category in ppm P: Olsen 11-16, Bray 1 25-45, Mehlich 1 20-40, Mehlich 3 30-50; in calcareous soil the Olsen optimum is higher, with over 25 ppm for zero P fertilizer.

A soil high in P by one test is generally high by another, though the numbers differ; low and medium levels mean likely yield gain from P, while high levels raise the potential for P pollution in runoff.
Tests capture P from recent manure and from soil minerals, but active organic matter from residues or manure may supply more P than the test shows.

sources.title: 21.6: Soil Testing for P - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))
21.5: Soil Testing for Nitrogen - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: In-season technologies that assess a crop's nitrogen status to guide fertilizer rates.

facts.text: Chlorophyll meters estimate leaf chlorophyll as an N indicator; they need field visits and adequate leaf sampling and are mainly used for final cereal applications.
Canopy reflectance sensors read near-infrared and red or red-edge light; mounted on equipment they adjust N on the go, usually with a high-N reference strip for calibration.
Satellite, aircraft or drone imagery uses the same bands at 10-30 m resolution; satellites are limited by cloud cover and aircraft and drones are more expensive.
Computer models simulate field N dynamics daily and are cheap and scalable, but involve no direct field observation.

sources.title: 21.5: Soil Testing for Nitrogen - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: Odd soil test values that usually trace to management history or to using the wrong extractant for the soil.

facts.text: Very high phosphorus comes from years of heavy poultry or other manure; very high pH with high calcium relative to K and Mg points to lime-stabilized sewage sludge.
High salt in humid regions can come from large poultry manure doses in high tunnels where rain cannot leach salts, or from deicing salt beside a road.
Acid extractants (Morgan, Mehlich 1 or 3) dissolve free limestone and give too much calcium, and on alkaline calcareous soils (pH above 7) they extract little P because the soil neutralizes the acid.
Many labs report the CEC the soil would have at pH 7 or higher, whereas the textbook estimates current CEC by summing the exchangeable bases.

sources.title: 21.9: Interpreting Soil Test Results - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: Labs sort each test value into categories from very low to excessive, each tied to the probability that adding the nutrient will raise yield.

facts.text: Categories run very low, low, optimum, high and excessive, with probability of response falling from very high to very low.
For the pre-sidedress nitrate test on corn 6-12 inches tall sampled to 1 foot, nitrate-N of 11-22 ppm is low, 23-28 optimum and over 35 excessive.
Ranges depend on the extractant: for Mehlich 3 in North Carolina, P is optimum at 26-50 ppm.
Reports adapt advice using the manure and previous crop information supplied; legume cover crop N is usually not credited and manure decided on later is missed.

sources.title: 21.10: Adjusting a Soil Test Recommendation - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))
21.11: Making Adjustments to Fertilizer Application Rates - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: Sampling a large field on a grid and analysing each point separately to guide site-specific nutrient and lime rates.

facts.text: The general recommendation is 2.5- to 5-acre grids, especially where manure and fertilizer rates varied; some areas use one-acre grids.
Unaligned grids are advised: points are shifted randomly off the regular grid so that a past applicator malfunction is not unknowingly sampled in a line.
Each grid point still needs 10-15 cores within about 30 feet.
Grid testing is expensive, so do it once per rotation, when lime may be needed, or every five to eight years; fertility patterns often do not follow soil survey maps.

sources.title: 21.12: Managing Field Nutrient Variability - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: High tunnel soils need adjusted tests because very high yields demand much more nutrient and rain does not leach salts.

facts.text: Tunnel tomatoes reaching the equivalent of 60-80 tons per acre need roughly 200-300 lb N, 300-400 lb P2O5 and 700-900 lb K2O per acre.
Recommendations from routine field soil tests must be adjusted upward, and a saturated media extract measures water-soluble nutrients including nitrate-N and ammonium-N plus total salinity.
